title: C-suite decision brief: predictable inference & risk mitigation
body:
Executive summary:

This brief is written for execs and procurement stakeholders evaluating dedicated inference capacity. It frames the purchasing decision around two non-negotiable customer outcomes: predictable throughput (measured as sustained qps and p99 tail latency under realistic request mixes) and risk transfer (isolation, fallbacks, and contractual remedies). The goal is to provide a short, negotiable set of commitments, a pragmatic measurement approach, and a negotiation playbook that procurement teams can use with customers and enterprise buyers.

Why this matters now:
- Customers are migrating mission-critical features (search, chat assistants, moderation) to LLMs; variability in inference can break user experience and revenue flows.
- Public cloud capacity variability and multi-tenant endpoints create unpredictable tail latency under bursty workloads.
- Buyers increasingly insist on SLOs plus operational practices (canarying, fallbacks, observability) instead of vague uptime promises.

High-level positioning statement for sales/AE:
"Redwood Dedicated gives you production-grade inference with contractual throughput and isolation guarantees so your critical AI features behave predictably under load — without re-architecting. We pair measurable SLAs with operational controls (reserved pools, autoscale guardrails, and model-variant fallbacks) so you get both reliability and cost clarity."

SLA constructs we recommend (negotiation-first):
1) Throughput SLA (primary):
   - Commitment: Reserved baseline throughput expressed as sustained tokens-per-second or concurrent inference slots (example: 12k tokens/sec sustained, burst to 18k tokens/sec up to 30s).
   - Measurement: 5-minute rolling windows, measured at the edge ingress (per-customer token rate), aggregated by calendar day.
   - Remedy: Service credits scaled to degree and duration of shortfall (tiered: 10% credit for 1 hour cumulative shortfall, 25% for >4 hours).

2) Latency SLO (secondary):
   - Commitment: p50/p95/p99 latency objectives per model family and per request type (e.g., prompt vs completion). Example baseline: p95 < 250ms for <512 tokens, p99 < 800ms for same workload.
   - Measurement: Observed at the inference gateway, excluding customer-side network variance; synthetic canaries + sampled production traces.
   - Remedy: Credits + expedited incident review; repeated breaches trigger escalation to priority remediation program.

3) Isolation & Resource Guarantee:
   - Commitment: Tenant isolation via reserved GPU pools and dedicated quota slices; noisy neighbor throttling policy described in appendix.
   - Measurement: Allocation logs and cluster placement snapshots (KPI: percent of requests served from reserved pool).
   - Remedy: Immediate capacity remediation plan plus proactive burst allowances during incidents.

4) Availability & Fallbacks:
   - Commitment: Measured availability of model-serving control plane (e.g., 99.95% monthly) and mandatory fallback pathways (smaller model, different region, cached responses) that keep best-effort service online.
   - Measurement: Control plane metrics + integration tests verifying fallback invocation.

Pricing & commercial framing:
- Offer a three-tier reserved SKU: Baseline reserve (committed throughput), Burst buffer (pay-as-you-go but with guaranteed priority), and Premium SLA (higher credits, shorter remediation timelines, on-call alignment).
- Tie credits to observable and auditable metrics. Avoid opaque language ("best efforts").
- For large deals, include an uplift for dedicated pool creation and a monthly minimum to cover fragmented utilization.

Procurement-ready clauses (strip for legal):
- Definition section: explicit definitions for "Tokens", "Sustained Throughput", "Burst Window", "Reserved Pool", and "Failure" (exclude customer misconfiguration).
- Measurement & audit: Redwood will provide daily and monthly usage/metric exports; buyer may request up to two independent audits per year (reasonable notice).
- Remedy ladder: credits scale by hours of sustained shortfall and by percentage short of promised throughput; continued noncompliance triggers right to terminate with pro-rated refund for unused reservation period.
- Operational commitments: 1) access to dedicated operational channel, 2) quarterly capacity review, 3) playbook for canary rollout & rollback.
- Data & security: standard controls (KMS, VPC peering, audit logs) with optional SOC/ISO artifacts as addendum.

Competitive analysis snapshot (quick):
- Large cloud managed endpoints: Often have elastic capacity but struggle to provide cost-predictable reserved pools and clear noisy-neighbor isolation in a way that buyers can contract against.
- Self-hosted inference vendors: Offer control but require heavy ops investment; our message: we provide equivalent isolation with Redwood-managed operational burden removed.
- API-first LLM providers: Great for fast prototyping but limited in enterprise-grade rollouts and contractual throughput guarantees.

Key differentiators to emphasize during procurement conversations:
- Quantified guarantees + operational playbook (not just "we will try").
- Built-in fallbacks and automatic model variant routing to avoid blackouts.
- Clear metering at token and request level for auditability.
- Route-level dashboards and cost/latency split — helps procurement and engineering agree on acceptance criteria.

Common buyer objections & suggested replies:
- "We can just overprovision in the cloud" → Overprovisioning hides the cost and still exposes you to multi-tenant variance; Redwood Dedicated isolates capacity and provides contractual remedies that budgeting teams can forecast.
- "We need guarantees across regions" → We support per-region reservations; propose a staged rollout with region-level baselines and cross-region failover documented in the SOW.
- "What if our traffic pattern changes?" → Provide a mechanism for rebaseline after a 30-day trend evaluation and offer tools to simulate peak shapes during contracting.

Negotiation playbook (practical steps):
1) Discovery: capture peak qps, 95/99 latency tolerance, token-per-request distribution, busiest 1% time windows.
2) Risk scoping: identify features that cannot tolerate >X ms or drop; map them to minimum reserved throughput.
3) Offer options: baseline reserve + burst buffer + fallback SLA. Present financial tradeoffs (chart: committed vs expected monthly spend vs cost of customer downtime).
4) Contract iteration: start with clear definitions and measurement, then iterate remedies and audit rights. Keep termination rights proportional to repeated SLA failures.
5) Operational handoff: include 60/90/120-day ramp checklist and a joint acceptance test (synthetic replay of buyer traffic inside a test window).

Metrics & KPIs to require in contract:
- Sustained throughput (tokens/sec) measured daily.
- p95/p99 latency for typical completion sizes.
- Percentage of requests served from reserved pool (target >95% during business hours).
- Mean time to remediation for capacity deficits (target <4 hours).
- Number of fallback activations and duration per month (should be low; used as signal).

Appendix (measurement methodology, quick notes):
- Use both synthetic canaries and production sampling for latency measurement; canaries provide cold-start observability while sampling captures real workload variance.
- Exclude outages clearly caused by buyer misconfiguration or network outages outside Redwood control. Capture examples in the SOW.
- Logging and export formats: daily CSV export with columns: timestamp, request_id, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency_ms, host_pool, reserved_pool_flag.

Open questions / action items: 
- Legal to draft minimal SLA language that can be parameterized per deal (Aisha, Legal lead).
- Product to sketch reserved-pool telemetry export (Liam) and define exact CSV schema.
- Sales to prepare two narrative playbooks: cloud migration vs net-new AI feature buy (Rina).
- Run a pilot contract template with 1 mid-market customer to validate measurement and remediation cadence (Diego to lead).

One-page TL;DR for executive email:
- Ask: Approve go-to-market standard SLA template and the three-tier commercial construct (Baseline + Burst + Premium).
- Why: Enables enterprise procurement to buy inference with predictable economics and contractual risk transfer.
- Risk if we do nothing: deals stall at procurement; buyers demand ad-hoc legal concessions and custom engineering for each large customer.
- Next: Legal + Product + Sales sync to produce the first SOW template and telemetry export within 3 weeks.

End notes: this document is a living draft — intended to be shared with Legal, Product, and 1–2 sales reps for iteration.
